name: Ernest Lawrence
paragraphs: Ernest Lawrence was the first UC Berkeley faculty member to receive a Nobel Prize. Lawrence joined Berkeley faculty in 1928 as an Associate Professor in Physics and became the youngest professor at the school. In 1929, he invented the cyclotron, winning him the Nobel Prize in Physics. The cyclotron accelerated particles to very high velocities without the use of high voltages, allowing for the discovery of radioactive isotopes. In 1931, Lawrence co-founded then-called Radiation Laboratory (Rad Lab), now the Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, which has hosted a number of future Nobel Laureates.

name: William Giauque
paragraphs: William Francis Giauque graduated from UC Berkeley’s College of Chemistry in 1920 and received his Ph.D. in chemistry and minor in physics in 1922. He became an Instructor of Chemistry in 1922 and was appointed as a professor in 1934. Giauque’s research on the behaviour of matter at temperatures close to absolute zero awarded him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1949.

name: Glenn Seaborg
paragraphs: Glenn Theodore Seaborg received his Ph.D. in Chemistry from UC Berkeley in 1937. He became an instructor of chemistry in 1939 and a professor in 1945. In 1946, Seaborg began leading nuclear chemical research at Radiation Lab. He served as the second Chancellor of UC Berkeley from 1958 to 1961, when President John F. Kennedy appointed him Chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission.
Seaborg and McMillan won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1951 for their co-discovery of plutonium and all further transuranium elements through element 102, including berkelium and californium.

name: Edwin McMillan
paragraphs: Edwin Mattison McMillan moved to UC Berkeley as a National Research Fellow in 1932. Later McMillan began working under Ernest Lawrence at the Radiation Lab. McMillan became an instructor in physics in 1935 and a professor in 1946.
Seaborg and McMillan won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1951 for their co-discovery of plutonium and all further transuranium elements through element 102, including berkelium and californium.

name: Emilio Segrè
paragraphs: Emilio Segrè came to Berkeley as a research associate at the Radiation Lab in 1938. Later, he joined the Physics Department as a lecturer. Segrè’s research initially focused on atomic spectroscopy, until he pivoted to researching nuclear physics. Segrè was recruited by Robert J. Oppenheimer and served as a group leader in the Los Alamos Laboratory of the Manhattan Project.
Segrè and Chamberlain primarily researched atomic and nuclear physics and received the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics for their discovery of the antiproton.

name: Owen Chamberlain
paragraphs: Owen Chamberlain joined the Manhattan Project in Los Alamos under Segrè in 1942 while pursuing his graduate degree at Berkeley. He returned to Berkeley in 1948 to accept a teaching position, and joined the Radiation Lab. Chamberlain continued to work with Segre, which led to their joint accolade. On campus, Chamberlain was also a supporter of the Free Speech Movement and advocated for minority enrollment at Berkeley.
Segrè and Chamberlain primarily researched atomic and nuclear physics and received the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics for their discovery of the antiproton.

name: Donald Glaser
paragraphs: Donald Arthur Glaser became a Professor of Physics at Berkeley in 1959. His research, conducted at the Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York and the Radiation Lab, focused on elementary particles. Glaser received the 1960 Nobel Prize in Physics for inventing the bubble chamber, which allowed scientists to track the paths of electrons, protons and other charged particles after collisions.

name: Melvin Calvin
paragraphs: Melvin Calvin started teaching at Berkeley in 1937 and became a Professor of Chemistry in 1947. Calvin became the Director of the Chemical Biodynamics Laboratory at Lawrence Radiation Laboratory in 1960. The Lab was renamed to the Melvin Calvin Laboratory in 1980 in his honor. Calvin received the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work at the lab on photosynthesis and research on the carbon dioxide assimilation in plants, now named the “Calvin Cycle.”

name: Luis Alvarez
paragraphs: Luis Walter Alvarez joined the Radiation Lab in 1936, later moving to the Los Alamos Lab as part of the Manhattan project, developing a detonator for the first nuclear weapon. After World War II, Alvarez came back to Berkeley, where he built and designed Berkeley’s 40-foot proton linear accelerator in 1947. He won the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physics for his continued research in elementary particle physics and his process of using the hydrogen bubble chamber.

name: Czesław Miłosz
paragraphs: Czesław Miłosz is Berkeley’s only Nobel Prize winner from the Division of Arts and Humanities. Miłosz, originally from Lithuania, wrote and published poetry as he sought refuge across Europe during World War II. UC Berkeley’s Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures invited Milosz to become a professor in 1960, a position he held until 1978, when he retired but continued to teach classes. Miłosz continued to write Polish poetry and literature centered around world conflict and repressive regimes, which won him the 1980 Nobel Prize in Literature.

name: Gerard Debreu
paragraphs: Gerard Debreu received the Rockefeller scholarship that allowed him to visit universities in the US, including UC Berkeley, in 1949. Debreu joined Berkeley as a Professor of Economics in 1962, and conducted research focusing on the theory of measure spaces of economic agents. Debreu received the 1983 Nobel Prize in Economics for creating formal mathematical models of economic equilibrium.

name: Yuan T. Lee
paragraphs: Yuen Tseh Lee received his Ph.D. from Berkeley in 1965. In 1974, Lee became a professor of chemistry at Berkeley and principal investigator at the Lawrence Radiation Laboratory. He served as the inaugural Co-Chair of the Chancellor’s Asian-American Affairs Committee in 1987. Lee won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his research in chemical elementary processes, with Dudley R. Herschbach and John C. Polanyi.

name: John Harsanyi
paragraphs: John Charles Harsanyi was appointed as a Visiting Professor and then Professor at the Business School and Department of Economics at Berkeley in 1964. Harsanyi was invited to help advise the United States Arms Control and Disarmament Agency where he identified incomplete-information in the situation, which led him to developing a mathematical procedure to convert incomplete-information games into a complete-information game. Harsanyi received the 1994 Nobel Prize in Economics with John F. Nash Jr. and Reinhard Selten for this analysis of equilibria in the theory of non-cooperative games.

name: Daniel McFadden
paragraphs: Daniel Little McFadden joined Berkeley’s faculty in 1963, yet moved to the economics faculty at MIT and became the Director of the Statistics Research Center in 1986. In 1991, McFadden returned to Berkeley to establish the Econometrics Laboratory. McFadden won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Economics with James J. Heckman for their research in analyzing how individuals maximize utility. McFadden continues to hold the E. Morris Cox Professor Emeritus of Economics title at Berkeley.

name: George Akerlof
paragraphs: George Arthur Akerlof received an assistant professorship at Berkeley in 1996. In his first year, wrote “Market for ‘Lemons,’” which was cited in his 2001 Nobel Prize in Economics. He became professor in 1978. Akerlof later received the 2001 Nobel Prize in Economics for his analyses of markets with asymmetric information, along with A. Michael Spence and Joseph E. Stiglitz. Akerlof went on to join the McCourt College School of Public Policy at Georgetown University, and recently retired.

name: George Smoot
paragraphs: George Fitzgerald Smoot accepted a position at Lawrence Radiation Laboratory in 1970. In 1988, Smoot co-led a research group that went on to launch the COBE satellite, which discovered variations in radiation in different directions, informing how stars form. Smoot received the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics with John C. Mather for this discovery.

name: Oliver Williamson
paragraphs: Oliver Eaton Williamson accepted an economics teaching position at UC Berkeley in 1963. After a tour of academic positions at the University of Pennsylvania and Yale, he returned to Berkeley in 1988, expanding his teaching to law. The Haas School established its highest faculty honor in his name: the Williamson Award. Williamson’s research focused on organizations, rather than markets, and he received the 2009 Nobel Prize in Economics for his analysis of economic governance.

name: Saul Perlmutter
paragraphs: Saul Perlmutter completed his Ph.D. in 1986 at Berkeley, continuing his research at UC Berkeley post-doc.  Perlmutter received the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics with Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess for their discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe through observations of distant supernovae. He served as the director of the Berkeley Institute for Data Science and is currently the executive director of the Berkeley Center for Cosmological Physics.

name: Randy Schekman
paragraphs: Randy W. Schekman joined Berkeley faculty in 1976, and received the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with James E. Rothman and Thomas C. Südhof for their discoveries of regulating vesicle transportation in cells. Schekman continues to teach Biology 1A at Berkeley.

name: Jennifer Doudna
paragraphs: Jennifer Anne Doudna became a professor of biochemistry and molecular biology and faculty at the Lawrence Berkeley National Lab in 2002. Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier developed a method of precise gene editing called CRISPR-Cas9, winning the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their research in 2020. Doudna also co-founded the Innovative Genomics Institute to research the potential of CRISPR and served as Li Ka Shing Chancellor’s Chair at Berkeley.

name: Reinhard Genzel
paragraphs: In 1980, Genzel joined Berkeley as a Miller Postdoctoral Fellow. A year later, he was appointed Associate Professor in the Physics Department. Genzel moved back to Germany in 1987 to become the director at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics. Genzel came back to Berkeley as part-time Professor in 1999, until 2016. Genzel has been an emeritus Professor since. Genzel received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics with Andrea Ghez for their discovery and proof of a black hole in the center of our Milky Way.

name: David Card
paragraphs: Class of 1950 Professor of Economics David Card received the 2021 Nobel Prize in Economics for his research on the labor market and effects of minimum wages, immigration and education. Card continues to support Ph.D. students at Berkeley through supervised independent study and research.

name: John Clarke
paragraphs: After completing a postdoctoral fellowship at UC Berkeley, John Clarke joined the Physics faculty and became a researcher at Lawrence Berkeley National Lab in 1969. He received the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics with Michel H. Devoret and John M. Martinis for discovering quantum mechanical properties on a macroscopic scale. Clarke is now a Professor Emeritus of the Graduate School in the Department of Physics.

name: Omar Yaghi
paragraphs: Omar M. Yaghi was appointed the James and Neeltje Tretter Chair Professor of Chemistry at Berkeley, and also serves as the Founding Director of the Berkeley Global Science Institute. Yaghi received the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Richard Robson and Susumu Kitagawa for their development of metal-organic frameworks. In July, Yaghi announced his leave from Berkeley to Tsinghua University, where he will lead an AI-driven materials research centre.
